The cover illustration emphasizes the importance of strengthening health system functions, such as disease surveillance and emergency health actions, to build climate resilience. The photograph depicts a health clinic in Nepal utilizing solar panels to ensure reliable energy access for essential medical services, even during extreme weather events. This publication was printed in Geneva, Switzerland. The operational framework for building climate-resilient health systems was prepared by experts from WHO and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), with financial support from the UK Department for International Development (DFID) and technical inputs from DFID representatives. The framework builds on existing WHO regional frameworks and work plans addressing climate change and health, such as those from the African, American, European, South-East Asian, Eastern Mediterranean, and Western Pacific regions. It also incorporates lessons learned from country projects funded by Norway, Germany, Spain, and the Global Environment Facility (GEF). WHO acknowledges the contributions of reviewers and participants from various meetings, including the DFID-funded project on climate change adaptation in health and the GEF/UNDP/WHO project on piloting health adaptation to climate change. These inputs were instrumental in finalizing the framework. The document introduces WHO’s operational framework for systematically addressing the health challenges posed by climate variability and change. It is designed for public health professionals, health managers, and decision-makers in related sectors such as nutrition, water, sanitation, and emergency management. International development agencies can also use this framework to guide investments and support for public health, health system strengthening, and climate change adaptation. The framework aims to enhance the capacity of health systems and public health programs to protect health in a changing climate. By implementing the ten key components outlined, health organizations and authorities can better anticipate, prevent, prepare for, and manage climate-related health risks. The public health rationale highlights clear evidence that human activities, particularly fossil fuel combustion and associated climate pollutants, are driving significant global climate changes. These changes have observable consequences on environmental and social conditions worldwide, presenting risks to human health. These risks are categorized into direct impacts (e.g., extreme weather events), environmental system-mediated impacts (e.g., air pollution, vector-borne diseases), and socially mediated effects (e.g., undernutrition, mental illness, population displacement). The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) identifies key reasons for concern, including the increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events, food system breakdowns, heightened risk of violent conflict, and economic slowdowns exacerbating poverty. Vulnerable populations, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, are disproportionately affected. Despite these challenges, mitigation and adaptation measures can significantly reduce health risks and protect environmental determinants of health. The framework is particularly relevant for health systems in lowand middle-income countries, which often face challenges in preparing for health emergencies, controlling disease burdens, and providing equitable healthcare. Building resilience in these settings requires addressing existing vulnerabilities within health systems. The operational framework aligns with global, regional, and national policy mandates, including WHO resolutions on health protection from climate change, strengthening health emergency management capacities, and implementing International Health Regulations. It also responds to requests from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) for support in planning climate change adaptation in key sectors, including health.
